newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Ousted Bhutto bids for third shot at power.
newsitem.headline: Ousted Bhutto bids for third shot at power.

text.p: Benazir Bhutto, twice elected and twice fired as prime minister of Pakistan, is battling against the odds to win a third term in Monday's elections.
Smarting from her unceremonious dismissal by President Farooq Leghari, a former ally, Bhutto hesitated before throwing her Pakistan People's Party (PPP) into the electoral fray.
She had hoped that the Supreme Court would reinstate her, despite her previous rows with the judiciary, just as it had restored her main rival, Nawaz Sharif, after his 1993 sacking.
But the court ruled last week that there was enough evidence of corruption, nepotism and other abuses to justify Leghari's action in sacking her three-year-old government.

Conventional wisdom says Sharif will ride to victory on a tide of public anger at the alleged corruption and misrule that marked Bhutto's last three years in office, but some voters may recall that his last government was sacked on the same grounds.
And Bhutto, the only woman to have reached the pinnacle of power in Pakistan, is a gritty fighter who thrives on adversity.
"The people of Pakistan will vote for a courageous leadership which brought an end to terrorism in Karachi," she declared at a rally on Saturday, the last day of campaigning.
A PPP spokesman dismissed as "rubbish" a Sunday Times report that she might be persuaded to take refuge in Britain if she loses the election to avoid a sensitive corruption trial.
The paper quoted Pakistani government sources as saying charges against Bhutto and her jailed husband, Asif Ali Zardari, would be dropped if she left the country and abandoned politics.
Zardari is held on a charge of conspiring in the murder of his wife's brother Murtaza in September. He denies the charge.
In a new twist to the political feuding within the Bhutto clan, Ghinwa Bhutto, Murtaza's Lebanese-born widow, has taken on the leadership of her husband's breakaway faction of the PPP.
Zardari, who was investment minister in his wife's cabinet, is seen as her biggest liability and prime target of an anti-corruption drive launched by the caretaker government.
Bhutto, who denies that Zardari had any hand in Murtaza's killing by Karachi police, has tried to divert attention from her spouse's alleged misdeeds by turning her guns on Leghari.
She accuses him of overstepping his powers and seeking to drag the military into politics by creating a new Council for Defence and National Security under his own chairmanship.
Bhutto argues that if such a council, which gives the generals a formal advisory role in government affairs, is needed, it should function under the prime minister.
"Under the constitution, there is no such role for the president and we will not accept such a role," she said.
Leghari says the council merely gives formal shape to an existing system of informal consultations with the military and will help ensure continuity after the elections.
"I was elected by the people of Pakistan and not by one man, but I have been dismissed by one man and not the people of Pakistan," Bhutto said, demanding that Leghari resign.
While in power, Bhutto had sworn to ride out the political and economic storms battering her government and seek a fresh mandate at elections she said would be held in October 1998.
She portrayed herself abroad as a woman struggling against the odds to steer her turbulent Islamic country on a moderate course of economic liberalisation and social justice.

The charismatic daughter of Pakistan's first popularly elected leader, Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, took over the PPP after her father was hanged in 1979 on the orders of former military ruler General Mohammed Zia-ul-Haq, who had toppled him in 1977.
For 11 years Bhutto fought vainly against Zia. Bhutto and her mother Nusrat were often in prison or under house arrest.
In August 1988 Zia died in a mystery air crash. Bhutto, weak from the birth of her first son, took to the hustings and the magic of the Bhutto name proved as potent as ever.
Her 1988 election victory was welcomed worldwide as the advent of democracy in Pakistan after more than a decade of military rule, but the establishment banded against her.
President Ghulam Ishaq Khan sacked her after just 20 months, accusing her of presiding over large-scale corruption.
She clawed her way back to power in the October 1993 election after three years in the political wilderness, only to be sacked a second time by a different president.
Bhutto, who wears an Islamic-style scarf on her head, was born on June 21, 1953 in Karachi, the first of four children.
She was educated at a Christian mission school in Karachi, Radcliffe (now part of Harvard) University, and Britain, where she became president of the Oxford Union debating society.
